fixes.explanation: Yes, friend, the text says it right out loud. The law covers a husband who suspects her, “…even though she has not defiled herself…” So the law looks at two situations, one where she has gone astray and one where she hasn't. Both start the same way, with a jealous husband and no witness. A hunch isn't a fact, and I once swore somebody swiped my last cookie when it was in my apron pocket the whole time.

Elders do show up in Israel (Exodus 3:16), but not in this law. Numbers 5:15 says the husband brings his wife to the priest. The priest is the one who then has her stand before the LORD and handles every step after that. So the elders can stay home for this one.

I see why you'd go there, since sacrifices come up a lot in the Bible. But this passage doesn't put blood in the jar. The text says the priest takes holy water in a clay jar and puts in some of the dust from the tabernacle floor (Numbers 5:17). Dust is the only thing it names for the jar at that point.

The text doesn't mention a covering here. It says the priest lets down her hair after she stands before the LORD, and then he places the grain offering in her hands (Numbers 5:18). It's easy to mix up, because the details come at you quick. The text doesn't tell us why he lets her hair down, so I won't make something up.

Foot washing is in the Bible (John 13:5), but not here. In this passage the priest lets down her hair after she stands before the LORD. Then he places the grain offering in her hands (Numbers 5:18). Nothing in these verses has the priest washing her feet.
Yes, “Amen, Amen.” That's the woman's whole answer after the priest speaks the curse over her (Numbers 5:22). One word, said twice. Sometimes the shortest line in the passage is the one that counts.

Yes, that's what the text says. The priest writes the curses on a scroll and washes them off into the bitter water (Numbers 5:23). That's the very water the woman is told to drink next (Numbers 5:24). I think this is a heavy part of the passage, so it's worth reading slowly.

Burning at the altar does show up in this passage, but it's the grain offering. The priest burns a handful of it as a memorial portion (Numbers 5:26). For the curses, the text says he writes them on a scroll and washes them off into the bitter water (Numbers 5:23). It doesn't mention the scroll going to the altar.

Almost, but the word "whole" is the catch. The text says the priest takes a handful of the grain offering as a memorial portion and burns that on the altar (Numbers 5:26). A handful, not the entire offering. It's a tiny detail, and it's easy to slide past.

Right, baker. The priest takes a handful of the grain offering as a memorial portion and burns it on the altar (Numbers 5:26). He doesn't burn the whole offering, just the handful. Good eye on a small detail.

A ram of atonement does appear a few verses earlier, in a different law (Numbers 5:8). This law ends with a different line about the husband. Verse 31 says he will be free from guilt. He isn't told to bring anything else here. Two laws in the same chapter, so I get the mix-up.
